wedge.question: My supplier raised prices. Should I pass it on?

copy.page_title: Shop cost decision — three options compared

world_verdict_labels.C: A 4% rise plus dropping low-margin lines

copy.headline: Your supplier put prices up {shock}%. Should you pass it on?
copy.hero_lede: We compared three decisions using the same model of your shop and the same assumptions. Only the decision changes between them — so the differences come from the decision, not from different guesses.

sens_help.low: Loyal customers, an awkward shop to replace, or competitors raising prices too.
sens_help.central: Our judgement: customers who could shop elsewhere, with some effort.
sens_help.high: Research figure for customers who can buy the identical item elsewhere.

copy.c_card_note: Depends on two of our assumptions: how much dropping low-margin lines cuts your {cost} (about {red} points here) and how many {unit} leave with those lines ({loss}%). Neither is calibrated to your business yet.
copy.chart_title: Cash in the bank under each decision
copy.chart_lede: Costs take about three weeks to rise — the stock on your shelves was bought at the old price. Customers react to a new price within a week or two.
copy.next_measurement: A two-week price test on a handful of lines — or your own sales figures from the last time you put prices up — would tell you far more about how your customers respond than any assumption we can make. That evidence can replace the estimate used here.
copy.sources_note: On price sensitivity: the research quoted measures customers switching between brands on the same shelf, which is easier than switching shops. It sets the top of the range rather than the middle, and the middle is our judgement, not a research finding.
limits_does_not: Predict the future or guarantee an outcome.
Model how competitors or marketplaces react.
Model advertising, search ranking or promotions.
Know your customers' price sensitivity — unless you bring evidence.

interventions.label: Raise retail prices
interventions.description: Adds the given number of percentage points to the average retail price for the whole horizon. Magnitude is the price increase in percent.

interventions.label: Stop restocking low-margin lines
interventions.description: Lowers average cost of goods per order by the given number of percentage points of the pre-shock cost, by shifting the mix away from lines that earn little, and costs a share of orders from customers who came for those lines. Magnitude is the cost reduction in percentage points; the demand cost is a fixed ratio of it (expert assumption, see the evidence registry).

event.label: Supplier prices +{shock}%
event.description: Wholesale / supplier prices rise and stay at the new level for 90 days.

options.label: Hold prices
options.headline: Keep your prices where they are and absorb the whole increase.

options.label: Raise prices 8%
options.headline: Pass most of the increase on with a 8% rise across the range.

options.label: Raise prices 4% + stop restocking low-margin lines
options.headline: A smaller 4% rise, plus letting the lines that earn least sell through and not reordering them.

registry_spec.label: Share of orders on low-margin lines
Price sensitivity of customers
registry_spec.assumption_source: No study supports this setting. bijmolt2005 and tellis1988 measure brand switching inside a shop and set the top of the range, not its middle.
registry_spec.note: A 1% price rise eventually reduces orders by this percentage. Low 0.70 / central 1.30 / high 2.60. Only the high setting is a published figure — the brand-level meta-analytic mean, i.e. customers who can buy the identical item elsewhere. The central and low settings are our judgement, set below brand level because changing shop is harder than changing brand. This is the assumption most likely to change the decision.

registry_spec.label: Share of supplier increase reaching your cost of goods
registry_spec.note: 100% by definition unless you can substitute cheaper lines, renegotiate, or hold fixed-price contracts (tested at 70%).

registry_spec.label: Delay before higher supplier prices reach your costs
registry_spec.note: Stock already on the shelf was bought at the old price. Tested over a 10-30 day range; the comparison uses the midpoint. A shop holding more stock than that sees the increase later than this shows.

registry_spec.label: How quickly customers react to a price change

map.slow: about two and a half weeks to half-react

registry_spec.label: Cost saving from dropping low-margin lines

value.text: {reduction:g} points off average cost of goods ({trim_effectiveness:.3f} per point of low-margin share)

registry_spec.note: Assumes low-margin lines carry roughly 2.9x the average cost share, which is close to what makes them low-margin. Tested at half and one-and-a-half times this rate.

registry_spec.label: Orders lost from dropping those lines
registry_spec.note: 0.45 of the cost saving, in points of orders: customers who came for the removed lines and do not substitute. Higher than the cafe's ratio because a shopper who cannot find a specific product is more likely to leave.

registry_spec.label: Price rises compared
registry_spec.note: The decisions being compared; fixed by the question.

registry_spec.label: Comparison horizon
registry_spec.note: Long enough for the stock to turn over at the new cost and for most of the customer reaction to land; short enough that rent and wages can be treated as fixed.

registry_spec.label: Average order value
registry_spec.note: Monthly sales divided by monthly orders.

sweep_labels.cogs_pass_through: How much of the supplier increase reaches your costs
sweep_labels.supplier_increase_pct: How large the supplier increase actually is
sweep_labels.trim_effectiveness: How much dropping low-margin lines really saves

sources.citation: Bijmolt THA, van Heerde HJ, Pieters RGM. New empirical generalizations on the determinants of price elasticity. Journal of Marketing Research. 2005;42(2):141-156.
sources.population: 1,851 price elasticities from 81 studies, predominantly packaged consumer goods in retail scanner data
sources.limitations: Brand-level in supermarket categories with near-perfect substitutes on the same shelf. It measures switching between brands inside a shop, not switching between shops.
sources.transfer: Used as the upper reference point. For a shop it is the 'my customers can buy the identical thing elsewhere' end of the range; for a cafe it is further away still, and the HIGH setting of 1.60 there is a judgement placed between the food category CI top (1.07) and this mean.

sources.citation: Tellis GJ. The price elasticity of selective demand: a meta-analysis of econometric models of sales. Journal of Marketing Research. 1988;25(4):331-341.
sources.population: 367 price elasticities from roughly 220 brands and markets
sources.limitations: Selective (brand-level) demand, largely goods rather than services, and estimated from studies published up to the mid-1980s. Like Bijmolt it measures brand switching, not store switching.
sources.transfer: A second brand-level reference point for the shop wedge, quoted so the range shown is not resting on a single meta-analysis. It does not establish what happens when one shop raises all of its prices at once.

intake_fields.label: Monthly sales
intake_fields.hint: Typical month, before the cost increase.

intake_fields.label: Orders per day
intake_fields.hint: Average orders or sales a day, online and in store together.

intake_fields.label: Monthly cost of goods
intake_fields.hint: What you pay suppliers for the goods you sell. Not wages, not rent, not shipping you absorb.

intake_fields.label: Monthly fixed costs
intake_fields.hint: Rent, wages, utilities, software, loan payments — everything that will not change in the next 90 days.

intake_fields.label: Cash available
intake_fields.hint: What is in the business account today.

intake_fields.label: Supplier cost increase
intake_fields.hint: The increase you are facing, as a percentage of what you pay for goods.

intake_fields.label: Share of orders on low-margin lines
intake_fields.hint: Roughly what share of orders are lines that earn you little. A guess is fine; it is tested as an assumption.

demo.name: Demo shop (fictional)
notes: Fictional. Chosen to be a realistic small retailer at a normal gross margin, not a composite of any real business.
Cost of goods is 58% of sales, so a 25% supplier increase removes roughly 14 points of gross margin if nothing else changes.

language.scenario_not_forecast: This is a scenario comparison under stated assumptions, not a forecast.
